<explanation>
Based on the complete file tree and the details in the README, you’re dealing with a system‐level, multi-architecture checkpoint/restore tool for Linux. The overall design is quite complex, as it not only provides the core userspace functionality to freeze and later restore processes, but also integrates several libraries (like libcompel for parasite injection and libsoccr for TCP connection handling) and supports a wide range of architectures (x86, ARM, MIPS, RISC-V, etc.) through dedicated directories.

Below is an explanation and step-by-step guidelines to create a detailed, accurate system design diagram for CRIU:

1. Identify the Main Components
   • Core Checkpoint/Restore Engine – This covers the “criu” directory, which contains the majority of the runtime code responsible for creating checkpoints, handling images, and restoring processes.
   • Parasite Injection Module – Represented by the “compel” directory and associated files; this library (libcompel) implements the technique of injecting code into a live process.
   • TCP Socket Handling – The “libsoccr” functionality, along with the “soccr” directory and related tests, support saving and restoring TCP socket states.
   • Architecture-Specific Modules – The project supports numerous architectures as indicated by directories like “compel/arch” and “criu/arch”. These modules provide low-level CPU- or kernel-specific code to cope with differences between various systems.
   • Plugins – CRIU is modular; the “plugins” directory and subdirectories (e.g., for amdgpu, cuda, etc.) extend the functionality with specific use-case extensions.
   • Supporting Libraries and Utility Code – This includes the “lib”, “include”, and “scripts” folders which provide auxiliary functions, public interfaces, build tools, and testing frameworks.
   • CI and Testing Infrastructure – With extensive CI configuration files (.github, .circleci, etc.) and “test” directories, it’s clear that automated building and testing are key aspects.

2. Define Interactions and Relationships
   • At the top, you can display an interaction between a running process (user application) and the CRIU engine. The engine “freezes” the process state by invoking system calls and then passing data between its internal modules.
   • The core checkpoint/restore engine then interacts with the parasite injection module (libcompel) to dynamically invoke code inside the running process.
   • Once a checkpoint is created, various image files (using the “images” folder and associated message definitions) are generated that capture process state, open file descriptors, memory mappings, and more.
   • During restore, the engine uses the same modules in reverse: reestablishing connections via libsoccr (for TCP sockets) and calling architecture-specific routines to set up the process’s CPU state.
   • The plugins come into play for specialized tasks (e.g., GPU/AMDGPU, CUDA) and extend the restoration process with additional, externally defined functionality.
   • At the bottom layer, common utility libraries and build scripts (Makefiles, configuration files) tie together various modules, while CI and test harnesses validate each component.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles
   • Modularity – The system is segmented into distinct modules (core engine, parasite injection, TCP state handling, plugins). Emphasize this separation in the diagram.
   • Abstraction per Architecture – A clear pattern is the use of “arch” directories in both CRIU and compel. This abstraction decouples architecture-specific code from the logic in the core engine.
   • Library-Driven and Plugin-Extensible – Libraries such as libcompel and libsoccr serve as standalone building blocks which the core engine leverages. Similarly, plugins provide additional functionality without modifying the core.
   • Automated Testing and Build Integration – While not part of the runtime path, the extensive CI setups and test folders are an indicator of continuous integration and validation cycles.

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram
   • Since this is a systems-level tool, make sure to group the components based on functionality:
     - A “Checkpoint/Restore Core” block.
     - A “Parasite Injection” block (libcompel) connected to the core.
     - A “Network State Handler” block (libsoccr) branching from the core.
     - “Architecture-Specific Adapters” grouped together – attach this block to the appropriate modules.
     - “Plugin Extensions” block that shows how additional plugins (e.g., for AMGPU, CUDA) hook into the engine.
     - A “Supporting Infrastructure” layer (libraries, include files, CI scripts, testing frameworks) that surrounds and underpins the main modules.
   • Use directional arrows to illustrate the flow:
     - From the user process to the core engine.
     - From the core engine to parasite injection and networking handlers.
     - Arrows indicating configuration flow from build scripts and CI to the various libraries.
   • Color Coding and Shapes:
     - Use distinct colors for “Core”, “Libraries”, “Plugins”, and “Architectural Adapters”.
     - Use boxes or rectangles for modules and rounded rectangles for external dependencies (such as the Linux kernel interfaces).
     - Label each block clearly (e.g., “CRIU Core”, “libcompel (Parasite Injection)”, “libsoccr (TCP Socket Restoration)”, “Architecture Modules”, “Plugin Extensions”).

5. Detailed Diagram Creation
   • Start the diagram with a box labeled “User Process/Application”.
   • Draw an arrow to a large block representing “CRIU Core Engine” (which encapsulates checkpoint creation, serialization, and restore operations).
   • Within or adjacent to the CRIU core, include sub-blocks:
       • “Parasite Injection Module (libcompel)” – show arrows from core engine to this module indicating that it is invoked to inject code into processes.
       • “Image Handler & Serializer” – a component that uses defined protocols (images directory and proto files).
       • “Process State Manager” – handling of memory mappings, file descriptors, etc.
   • Parallel to these modules, draw a block labeled “TCP Connection State (libsoccr)” and connect it to the core engine.
   • On the side, aggregate architecture-specific modules in one group (listing supported architectures like x86, arm, etc.).
   • Finally, draw an external “Plugin Framework” block that interfaces with the core engine to extend functionality.
   • Optionally add a lower-tier section for “Build & Test Infrastructure” indicating integration with CI systems and automated testing.

By following these steps and guidelines, your diagram will capture the essential architectural elements of CRIU, delineate responsibilities clearly, and communicate both the modular design and the interactions between the main components. This detailed and color-coded diagram will provide a clear visual representation of the complex, multi-layered system that is central to CRIU’s purpose of checkpointing and restoring Linux tasks.
</explanation>
